messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts:
We've talked about the need for a statistical testing framework in Stan to ensure that
we're getting reasonable estimates on a variety of test models.  This needs to go
beyond what we currently do in the model tests, which only checks first-order
expectations.

What we really want to do is check the Monte Carlo sampling distribution itself,
in other words that Delta \equiv ( \hat{mu} - mu_{true} ) / MCSE ~ N(0, 1).  This requires that
we have valid estimates of both the Monte Carlo mean, \hat{mu}, and the
Monte Carlo variance and autocorrelation implicit in the MCSE.

The most obvious way to test this would be a simple two-sided Gaussian hypothesis test
for Delta < n for some n \in Z^{+}.  The problem here is that if n is small then we'll get many
false rejections and if n is large then we won't be as sensitive to the shape of the Delta
distribution.

As a more robust test I propose instead the following procedure.

For each model, build up the test by running multiple chains with random initializations.

(Not immediately related to statistical validity, but we would throw in a convergence
test at this point as well).

For each chain compute Delta_{i}.

For n = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} compute a two-sided Binomial test on | Delta_{i} | < n using
the known two-sided Gaussian probabilities. Tune the test to a p-value of 1e-3
to avoid too many rejections.

The hope is that this approach gives us strong sensitivity to the shape of the distribution 
of Monte Carlo estimates (both in the bulk and in the tails) without having two many
false rejections that would make incorporating these into any frequently-runt test
a pain.

Thoughts?  Am I doing anything stupid statistically (i.e. is this actually better than
just doing a two-sided Gaussian test directly)?

-Betancourt

parts:
I hope somebody who knows more than me can reply to this and
we can start doing something about it. People must've looked
at this. I know Andrew likes his work with Cook and Rubin.

What's Delta (just the draws(s))? And how do we ensure we have
valid estimates of the mean and MCSE? We could just trust Rhat and n_eff,
but that's rather circular!

It seems the other test we could do was create bins and run
a chi-square test. I have no idea about the strengths of all
these tests, though.

I've been trying to keep these open design docs on the wiki
so everyone can correct and comment on them.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts:
I think there are a lot of ways of doing this. I have no feeling that what I did with Cook and Rubin is optimal. Rather, my point is that some issues came up in figuring these things out, and it might be that by reading the paper, we can get a sense of the steps that are required. I suspect this will work better than starting from scratch and rediscovering all the problems for this new example.

Also, I'm interested in this topic for a similar reason as to why I'm interested in efficiency comparisons and R-hat: these are all ways of applying statistical data analysis to the output of simulations.
A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts: What's Delta (just the draws(s))?
Delta is (mean - true) / MCSE.  If our sampler is valid it will have a N(0, 1) distribution.

And how do we ensure we have
valid estimates of the mean and MCSE?  
We could just trust Rhat and n_eff,
but that's rather circular!

We are not testing convergence here.  We are assuming convergence and testing
the validity of the Monte Carlo estimate.

It seems the other test we could do was create bins and run
a chi-square test.  I have no idea about the strengths of all
these tests, though.

I do _not_ want to test the distribution of the drawn samples.  That's asking for all
kinds of problems.  All I want to do is ensure that the coverage of the Monte Carlo
estimates is correct (i.e. consistent with the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem)
without having a blight of false rejections.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts:
Let me be more clear here.  As I noted in my reply to Bob, I do not want to test for the consistency of the sampled distribution (a sum of point masses)
to the true distribution.  The difficulty in testing the entire distribution (for example KS, or the quantile test in the Cook et al. paper) is that it is
extremely sensitive to convergence and the independence of the samples.  This makes it hard to determine test coverage and tune the tests so that
they reject only when something is wrong.

The more robust measure here is the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem, which states that (mean - true) / MCSE ~ N(0, 1).  This incorporates
autocorrelation and is less sensitive to the fine details of convergence.  We also don't want to limit ourselves to a single test because of the difficulty
with the rejection rate, hence the use of an ensemble of chains and turning the whole shebang into a binomial test at various z-scores.

On Wed, Feb 5, 2014 at 3:35 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
I think there are a lot of ways of doing this.  I have no feeling that what I did with Cook and Rubin is optimal.  Rather, my point is that some issues came up in figuring these things out, and it might be that by reading the paper, we can get a sense of the steps that are required.  I suspect this will work better than starting from scratch and rediscovering all the problems for this new example.

Also, I'm interested in this topic for a similar reason as to why I'm interested in efficiency comparisons and R-hat:  these are all ways of applying statistical data analysis to the output of simulations.
A

>
> What's Delta (just the draws(s))?
>

> Delta is (mean - true) / MCSE. If our sampler is valid it will have a N(0, 1) distribution.

I see --- mean is the posterior mean from the sampler
for a quantity of interest, like a parameter mean or
variance?

> valid estimates of the mean and MCSE?

> but that's rather circular!

Don't we need to estimate "true" somehow? You're just
thinking a really long run? We'd want to test convergence
for that, right?

But wouldn't that (mean - true)/MCSE only be normal after
convergence? And if so, doesn't that implicitly test
convergence? Or does the MCSE take into account not
converging, too?

> It seems the other test we could do was create bins and run
> a chi-square test. I have no idea about the strengths of all
> these tests, though.
>
>
> I do _not_ want to test the distribution of the drawn samples. That's asking for all
> kinds of problems. All I want to do is ensure that the coverage of the Monte Carlo
> estimates is correct (i.e. consistent with the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem)
> without having a blight of false rejections.

I wasn't thinking about that so much as testing the posterior
quantities of interest for a bunch of runs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework

On Wednesday, February 5, 2014 3:04:09 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We are not testing convergence here.  We are assuming convergence and testing
> the validity of the Monte Carlo estimate.

Don't we need to estimate "true" somehow?   You're just
thinking a really long run?  We'd want to test convergence
for that, right?

We can do all the conjugacy examples and thereby know what is true in those cases, but it is still necessary to run the test long enough to where convergence can be assumed.

But for the multiparameter models, we really would want to test the validity with respect to a multivariate normal, right? That was basically how Andrew found the problem with the previous Stan that the covariance matrix of the coefficients was off.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts:
>>
>> Delta is (mean - true) / MCSE. If our sampler is valid it will have a N(0, 1) distribution.
>
> I see --- mean is the posterior mean from the sampler
> for a quantity of interest, like a parameter mean or
> variance?
Correct.

>> We are not testing convergence here. We are assuming convergence and testing
>> the validity of the Monte Carlo estimate.
>
> Don't we need to estimate "true" somehow? You're just
> thinking a really long run? We'd want to test convergence
> for that, right?

True would come from the model. The idea is to mimic a unit test — we isolate
a pathology in the simplest possible model that still manifests it and then include
that in our tests. So, for example, IID gaussian, correlated gaussian, the funnel,
maybe the banana, etc.

> But wouldn't that (mean - true)/MCSE only be normal after
> convergence? And if so, doesn't that implicitly test
> convergence? Or does the MCSE take into account not
> converging, too?

We’d have to assume convergence. Note that I mentioned a convergence tests
first, as in we check all the Rhats before running the statistical validity tests
(using the same chain output). Of course, if the Rhats look fine but the Monte
Carlo Central Limit Theorem is not holding then we have bigger issues!

>> I do _not_ want to test the distribution of the drawn samples. That's asking for all
>> kinds of problems. All I want to do is ensure that the coverage of the Monte Carlo
>> estimates is correct (i.e. consistent with the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem)
>> without having a blight of false rejections.
>
> I wasn't thinking about that so much as testing the posterior
> quantities of interest for a bunch of runs.

Recall that Monte Carlo is all about computing expectations, so “posterior quantities of
interest” are all expectations by definition (this, however, includes almost anything
if framed correctly).

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
parts: > But for the multiparameter models, we really would want to test the validity with respect to a multivariate normal, right? That was basically how Andrew found the problem with the previous Stan that the covariance matrix of the coefficients was off.

No, the problem Andrew found was in a 2D gaussian with independent components. Because the variance was
off this would lead to a rejection in the framework I proposed. Besides, if the covariance matrix was suspect
we could just test individual components.
